relationship: Narrative parallel: hiding objects of foreign worship
rationale: Isaiah says the handmade things will be hidden; the preceding description identifies objects made by fingers and worshiped, and the following unit locates their concealment in caves and earth. Genesis describes Jacob hiding the foreign gods surrendered by his household beneath the terebinth. Both passages remove worshiped objects from sight, although Genesis additionally says Jacob destroyed them and Isaiah's unit does not assert destruction.

relationship: Thematic parallel: divine law as sustaining help
rationale: Isaiah explicitly says that God gave law for help, in contrast with the utterance discussed after consulting the dead. The psalmist says meditation on God's law kept him from perishing in humiliation, that the ordinances gave him life, and asks for salvation while seeking them. The connection is the law's beneficial, sustaining function; the psalm does not resolve Isaiah's unusual clause about gifts or replace it with another wording.

relationship: Restoration parallel: Israel turning toward its God
rationale: Isaiah places Jacob's remainder toward a mighty God, immediately after the promise that the survivors will trust Israel's Holy One instead of those who wronged them. Hosea says Israel's sons will return and seek the Lord their God after their long deprivation. Both envisage a renewed orientation of Israel toward God; Hosea adds seeking David their king and does not supply the title mighty God.

relationship: Judgment imagery: a national blow without healing
rationale: Within the lament against Babylon's king, Isaiah describes a nation struck by an incurable, unsparing blow. Nahum describes crushing without healing and an inflamed wound, while hearers clap over the one whose evil continually reached others. The royal-judgment passages use bodily injury without healing to portray devastating violence; Isaiah's nation receiving the blow is not identified with Nahum's addressee, and the direction of the injury differs.

relationship: Royal parallel: granted glory with general submission
rationale: Isaiah promises Eliakim David's glory and rule with no one contradicting. Chronicles describes Solomon occupying David's throne, receiving obedience from Israel and submission from the rulers, while the Lord gives him exceptional royal glory. Both connect granted Davidic honor with accepted rule. Eliakim and Solomon remain distinct figures, and no key or opening-and-shutting language is supplied to Isaiah.

relationship: Lament imagery: drinking turned to bitterness
rationale: Isaiah replaces the surrounding wine-associated gladness with shame and sikera bitter to its drinkers. The lamenting speaker describes public mockery and being filled with bitterness and made drunk with gall, followed by the loss of peace and good things. Both portray affliction through bitter drinking rather than enjoyment; the comparison does not identify sikera with gall or claim the same drink or occasion.

relationship: Rhetorical comparison: receiving as one has inflicted
rationale: Isaiah asks whether the unnamed figure will be struck and killed just as he himself struck and killed. Obadiah declares that the addressee will receive recompense corresponding to what he did. The shared comparison sets received harm beside inflicted harm, but Isaiah poses a question beginning Surely he will not, whereas Obadiah makes an affirmative announcement. The comparison neither settles Isaiah's pronouns nor turns the question into Obadiah's assertion.

relationship: Contextual parallel: mutual support among makers of worship objects
rationale: Isaiah's neighbor-and-brother help is immediately developed through the craftsman, hammering smith, joining, and objects secured with nails. In Acts, the maker of silver Artemis shrines gathers related craftsmen to defend their work against the teaching that handmade things are not gods. Both scenes place collective support around making worship objects; Acts specifies commercial interests and Artemis, which are not supplied as the identities or motives of Isaiah's workers.

relationship: Memorial imagery: represented Israel kept before the Lord
rationale: To answer Zion's fear of being forgotten, God says He painted her walls on His hands and keeps her continually before Him. Exodus orders Israel's sons' names engraved on stones carried on Aaron's shoulders before the Lord as a memorial. Both use a bodily borne representation to express continuing remembrance before God. The painted walls on God's hands remain distinct from engraved names on priestly shoulder stones.

relationship: Theological contrast: God's righteousness and human wrongdoing
rationale: Isaiah distinguishes God's own righteousness from the people's evils, which cannot benefit them. Daniel's confession similarly assigns righteousness and mercy to the Lord, while assigning shame to the people because they sinned, fell away, and disobeyed His law. God's accusation and Daniel's confession occupy different speaking positions but preserve the same contrast; neither text calls the human evils God's righteousness.

relationship: Image parallel: a spider's web and the futility of ungodliness
rationale: Isaiah describes lawless people weaving a spider's web, whose inability to provide clothing is explained in the next unit. Bildad depicts the ungodly person's tent becoming a spider's web and his propped-up house failing to stand. In both arguments the web exposes the uselessness of what the ungodly produce or rely on. Job's statement belongs to Bildad's speech; it does not establish that Job is ungodly or explain Isaiah's separate asp-egg and basilisk imagery.

relationship: Restoration imagery: people compared with doves
rationale: Isaiah asks about arrivals flying like clouds and doves with their young, within the gathering of Zion's children from far away. Hosea compares those from Egypt and Assyria's land with a bird and a dove and promises to restore them to their houses. Both restoration scenes employ bird imagery for returning people. Hosea's verb is astonished, not flying, and Isaiah's young are not replaced with windows or a dovecote.

relationship: Within-book literary parallel: Zion astonished at newly given children
rationale: Isaiah 66 asks how a nation could be born all at once and declares that Zion labored and bore her children. In Isaiah 49, the formerly childless and widowed Zion asks who bore and raised the unexpectedly numerous children now needing room. Both depict restored Zion as a mother astonished at her children. Chapter 49 does not repeat the one-day timing or establish how the sudden birth occurs.
